body_html:
Insurance appraisal for hail damage claims is a policy-based process for resolving disputes over how much hail damage exists and what repairs cost. When your insurer accepts a hail claim but underpays it, either side can demand appraisal, each appoints an appraiser, and an umpire settles any remaining differences in a binding award.

Texas sees more hail claims than almost any other state. From the DFW Metroplex to Central Texas and the Panhandle, spring and early summer storms routinely damage roofs, siding, windows, gutters, and HVAC units across entire neighborhoods. When thousands of claims hit at once, disagreements over scope and price are inevitable.

This guide explains why hail claims so often end up in appraisal, how the process works step by step, what evidence matters most, and how to avoid the mistakes that weaken a hail appraisal.

What Is Insurance Appraisal for Hail Damage?

Most Texas homeowners and commercial property policies include an appraisal clause. It applies when you and the insurer agree there was a covered loss but fail to agree on the amount of loss. For hail claims, that usually means the carrier accepts that a storm hit the property but disputes how much of the roof or exterior was damaged, whether repair or replacement is needed, or what the work costs.

Appraisal is not a lawsuit. It is a contractual process run by appraisers and, if needed, an umpire. Under State Farm Lloyds v. Johnson (Tex. 2009), a hail case, the Texas Supreme Court confirmed that appraisers can decide the extent of hail damage to a roof, while questions of coverage stay with the insurer and the courts. For a full overview, see what is an insurance appraisal.

Why Do Hail Damage Claims End Up in Appraisal?

Hail claims generate more appraisal demands than almost any other type of property loss. The most common reasons:

  • Repair vs replacement. The carrier approves a few slopes or a handful of shingles; the homeowner's contractor says the whole roof needs replacement.
  • Functional vs cosmetic damage. Insurers may label hail marks as cosmetic. Learn the difference in what is functional damage in roof claims.
  • Missing line items. Starter, drip edge, flashing, ridge vents, and code items often fall out of the scope.
  • Low measurements or waste. Small errors in squares or waste factor add up on large roofs.
  • Matching. Insurers may refuse to replace undamaged siding or shingles that no longer match the repaired area.
  • Collateral damage overlooked. Gutters, downspouts, window screens, fences, and AC fins get left off.
  • Pricing. Post-storm labor and material costs climb faster than estimating software reflects.

How the Hail Damage Appraisal Process Works

StepWhat happensYour focus
1. DemandYou or the insurer sends a written appraisal demand under the policyFollow the clause's notice requirements
2. Appraisers namedEach side names a competent, independent appraiserChoose someone with hail and roofing expertise
3. Umpire selectedThe appraisers agree on an umpire, or a court appoints oneYour appraiser vets umpire candidates
4. InspectionAppraisers inspect the roof, elevations, and interior if neededProvide access, photos, and storm documentation
5. Estimate comparisonLine-by-line negotiation of scope, quantities, and priceSupply contractor estimates and supporting evidence
6. AwardTwo of three sign an award setting the amount of lossReview the award and payment timing

Timelines vary with the size of the loss and how quickly appraisers and umpires are named. Many residential hail appraisals resolve in a matter of weeks to a few months. See how long an insurance appraisal takes for what affects the schedule.

Line items frequently missed on hail roof estimates

  • Starter course at eaves and rakes
  • Drip edge, especially where local code requires it
  • Step, counter, and chimney flashing (see why flashing is commonly missed in claims)
  • Ridge vents, turtle vents, and pipe jacks
  • Steep-slope and high-roof labor charges
  • Satellite dish and solar panel detach and reset
  • Gutter guards, downspouts, and soft-metal items

Hidden Hail Damage and Functional Damage

Hail damage is not always obvious. Impacts can fracture the shingle mat or dislodge granules in ways that are hard to see from the ground but shorten the roof's life and lead to leaks. Damage to underlayment or decking may not show until tear-off. On commercial roofs, hail can crack membranes or crush insulation boards beneath an intact-looking surface.

Hail also damages more than roofs. Siding can crack or dent, window screens and frames can tear, wood fences and decks can show spatter marks, and outdoor AC coil fins can be crushed. Each of these belongs in the scope if the storm caused it, and each is easy to overlook when an inspection focuses only on the roof.

That is why careful, close-up inspection matters. Experienced appraisers look for bruising, fractured mats, exposed fiberglass, and patterns consistent with a single storm, then compare them to collateral damage on soft metals and other surfaces.

Tip: Ask for the adjuster's photos and test-square notes. If the adjuster inspected only one or two slopes, request that the remaining slopes be documented before you accept the scope.

What Documentation Wins Hail Appraisal Disputes?

Hail appraisals turn on evidence. The most useful documentation includes:

  1. Date-of-loss storm data, such as National Weather Service or NOAA storm reports for your area.
  2. Dated photos of every roof slope, elevation, and collateral item, with chalk circles and scale references.
  3. Measurement reports from aerial, drone, or field measurements, including pitch and waste.
  4. Itemized contractor estimates, not lump-sum bids.
  5. Matterport 3D or drone documentation that captures the condition of the whole property.
  6. All correspondence with the insurer, including estimates, denial or partial denial letters, and engineer reports.

Our claim documentation checklist helps you gather everything in one place.

Matching and Building Codes in Hail Claims

Two issues routinely inflate the gap between carrier and contractor estimates on hail claims.

Matching. When hail damages part of a roof or one elevation of siding, replacement materials often cannot match the remaining product because of discontinued colors or weathering. Whether your policy pays to replace undamaged areas for uniformity depends on its language and the facts. Strong matching evidence includes product identification, manufacturer discontinuation notices, and side-by-side photos showing visible differences in color, profile, or exposure between new and existing materials. Appraisers weigh that evidence when deciding the scope needed to restore the property to a reasonably uniform appearance.

Code upgrades. A full re-roof may trigger current code requirements such as drip edge, underlayment specifications, or ventilation. Coverage for those upgrades usually depends on ordinance or law coverage in your policy.

Hail Appraisal vs Public Adjuster vs Lawsuit

  • Public adjuster: represents you throughout the claim and negotiates with the insurer, but cannot force a number.
  • Appraisal: produces a binding amount of loss through appraisers and an umpire, usually faster and cheaper than court.
  • Lawsuit: may be needed for coverage denials or bad-faith conduct. Texas weather claims generally require 61 days' pre-suit notice under Insurance Code chapter 542A.

Many hail disputes never need litigation once the amount of loss is set by appraisal. Paying an appraisal award does not automatically end every claim, though. In Barbara Technologies v. State Farm Lloyds (Tex. 2019), the Texas Supreme Court held that payment of an award does not by itself bar a prompt-payment claim, while Ortiz v. State Farm Lloyds (Tex. 2019) held that payment generally bars most other extra-contractual claims. This is general information, not legal advice.

What happens after the hail appraisal award?

The award typically lists the replacement cost value and actual cash value for each category of damage. The insurer then pays according to the policy, subtracting your deductible and any prior payments. If your policy pays replacement cost, the recoverable depreciation is usually released after repairs are completed and documented. Our recoverable depreciation calculator helps you estimate what is still owed after the actual cash value payment.

Why Texas Hail Claims Are Different

Texas hail season peaks in spring and early summer, though damaging storms can occur well outside that window. North Texas, the Panhandle, and Central Texas see frequent large-hail events, and a single storm can damage tens of thousands of roofs across a metro area.

That scale shapes claims. Carriers bring in outside adjusters, inspections get rushed, and demand for roofers spikes prices. Many policies in Texas also carry percentage-based wind and hail deductibles, so a scope that looks only slightly low can push a claim below the deductible entirely. Homeowners in Dallas, Fort Worth, and the surrounding suburbs see these dynamics most often.

Common Mistakes in Hail Damage Appraisal

  • Waiting too long to document damage or challenge the estimate, allowing later storms to muddy causation.
  • Relying on phone calls instead of written requests and responses.
  • Using a contractor as your appraiser, which can violate the policy's independence requirement.
  • Replacing the roof before documenting every slope and collateral item.
  • Accepting the first umpire suggested without vetting their background.

Next Steps Before You Invoke Appraisal on a Hail Claim

  1. Request the insurer's full estimate, photos, and measurement report.
  2. Get at least one itemized contractor estimate.
  3. Compare line items to find scope, quantity, and pricing gaps.
  4. Run the numbers through our appraisal cost calculator.
  5. Talk to an experienced appraiser before sending a demand.

Questions to ask a potential hail appraiser

  • How many hail roof claims have you inspected and estimated in Texas?
  • Do you write your own line-item estimates in Xactimate or Symbility?
  • How do you document functional damage and collateral evidence?
  • How do you vet umpire candidates?
  • What is your fee structure, and what costs should I expect?

faqs.q: Can I use appraisal if my insurer only approved a partial roof repair?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. When the insurer accepts hail damage but approves only some slopes or shingles, the disagreement is about the extent of damage and the amount of loss. Texas courts have held that appraisers can decide how much of a roof hail damaged. Your appraiser documents the remaining damage and negotiates the scope with the insurer's appraiser.

faqs.q: How much does hail damage appraisal cost?
faqs.a: Under most Texas policies, each side pays its own appraiser and the two sides split the umpire's fee. Appraiser fees vary based on the size and complexity of the claim. Before invoking appraisal, compare the expected cost to the gap between the insurer's estimate and a realistic repair cost, and ask any appraiser for a clear fee structure upfront.

faqs.q: What if the insurer says my hail damage is only cosmetic?
faqs.a: Cosmetic damage affects appearance, while functional damage affects how the roof sheds water or how long it lasts. Some Texas policies include cosmetic damage exclusions, especially for metal roofs. If you believe the damage is functional, document fractured mats, granule loss, and exposed fiberglass. Whether damage is functional often becomes a central issue in hail appraisal.

faqs.q: Does a second hailstorm affect my appraisal?
faqs.a: It can. If another storm hits before the first claim is resolved, the insurer may argue that some damage came from the later event or that it was already present. Prompt documentation with dated photos and storm reports helps separate the losses. Appraisers may need to allocate damage between events, which is why acting quickly matters.
